strengths: Principled and elegant mathematical formulation: The paper addresses a known limitation in group-equivariant vision networks—namely, that saturation and luminance lie on bounded intervals rather than groups—by lifting the interval to a circle via a double-cover map. This cleanly eliminates the clipping and zero-padding artifacts present in prior work (such as LCER).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The authors evaluate equivariance error both qualitatively and quantitatively (demonstrating near-zero numerical error), test out-of-distribution generalization across individual and joint HSL shifts on synthetic benchmarks (3D Shapes, Small NORB), and validate on real-world medical imaging (Camelyon17) and shifted natural image datasets.

Insightful analysis of representation geometry: The paper does not merely propose the architecture; it thoroughly analyzes the implications of the double-cover, including the occurrence of redundant representations, lifting coverage, and introduces an entropy-density metric to guide the selection of group order.

Exemplary honesty regarding limitations: The authors explicitly evaluate and characterize settings where color equivariance is counterproductive, such as when color is the predictive signal (tested on tomato ripeness in KUTomaData) or when no distribution shift exists (analyzing the capacity trade-off from filter-depth reduction).
weaknesses: Unnatural semantic topology for bounded physical quantities: Wrapping a bounded interval (like saturation or luminance) into a circle means that shifting past the boundary reflects or wraps around (e.g., continually increasing saturation causes it to cycle back down). While this achieves algebraic group structure and perfect equivariance mathematically, physical color shifts do not behave cyclically. The paper would benefit from discussing the semantic implications of this artificial periodicity in downstream tasks.

Steep computational and memory scaling: Because group convolutions on product groups scale with the product of group cardinalities ($N \times M \times R$), full HSL equivariance ($H_4 S_4 L_4$, order 64) incurs a massive computational burden. As documented in Table 12, memory explodes from ~1 GB to ~33 GB and speed drops by over an order of magnitude for a small ResNet-18 backbone, posing practical hurdles for scaling to modern backbones or higher resolutions.

Mixed results against data augmentation on natural benchmarks: On several shifted benchmarks in Table 6, specialized data augmentation baselines (such as AugMix or Planckian Jitter) perform comparably to or better than $\mathbb{T}^3$CEN (e.g., Caltech-101 and Oxford Pets), and Table 9 shows that enforcing equivariance leads to performance drops on in-distribution data due to reduced channel capacity.

Underdeveloped discussion on geometric extensions: The extension of the double-cover mechanism to scale equivariance in Section 6 is interesting but only backed by qualitative feature maps (Figure 8). A more rigorous quantitative experiment on scale benchmarks would substantiate this claim.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant challenge in group equivariant deep learning: handling interval-valued, non-cyclic color channels (saturation and luminance) where boundary clipping in previous translation-based methods causes approximation artifacts.

The experimental evaluation covers a diverse set of tasks and datasets, including synthetic benchmarks (3D Shapes), lighting variations (small NORB), medical imaging (Camelyon17), and common real-world vision benchmarks (CIFAR, STL-10, Caltech-101, Stanford Cars, Oxford Pets).

Section 5.5 provides an honest and insightful discussion of the failure modes and boundaries of color equivariance, analyzing scenarios where color is predictive of the label (KUTomaData) and the capacity tradeoffs when there is no distribution shift.
weaknesses: Mathematical invalidity of the covering map: The central theoretical construction claims to use a 'topological covering' via $\pi(\theta) = \frac{c}{2} \sin \theta$ from $\mathbb{T}^1$ to $[-c/2, c/2]$. In topology, a covering map must be a local homeomorphism where every base point has an evenly covered neighborhood. Because $\pi'(\theta) = \frac{c}{2} \cos \theta$ vanishes at $\theta = \pm \pi/2$, the map folds over at the boundaries $\pm c/2$, which fail to have evenly covered neighborhoods. It is a folded projection/branched map, not a covering map.

Unphysical group action: Natural saturation and luminance are bounded monotonic photometric quantities. Enforcing a cyclic group action $C_M$ via $\sin$ causes saturation and luminance to oscillate sinusoidally back and forth between minimum and maximum values when shifting along the group orbit. This periodic wrap-around does not correspond to physical illumination or color variations, and results in redundant representations where up to half the lifted channels are mirrored duplicates (as acknowledged in Section 5.4).

Fundamentally flawed extension to scale equivariance: In Section 6 (Equation 24), the paper claims to extend the framework to spatial scale equivariance by defining the action on pixel coordinates as $(\pi((p_x + g_i) \pmod{2\pi}), \pi((p_y + \alpha_i) \pmod{2\pi}))$. Passing spatial coordinates through phase-shifted sine functions scrambles spatial geometry and has no relation to spatial dilation/scaling, rendering the claim of scale equivariance mathematically invalid.

Tautological equivariance error evaluation: The reported near-zero equivariance error ($4.66 \times 10^{-6}$ in Figures 3 and 10) is measured strictly against the authors' artificially defined cyclic group action. Because a discrete group convolution over a finite cyclic group is equivariant by construction up to floating-point precision, this metric does not demonstrate robustness to real-world continuous saturation/luminance shifts.

Presentation and notation issues: The paper contains several editorial errors, including mismatched cross-references (the text on page 6 refers to Table 8 for HSL shifts on 3D Shapes, but the data is in Table 4; Table 8 on page 8 is hue-shift MNIST), unexplained notation shifts (referring to '$T^4$CEN' on page 9), index typos in Equation 24 ($g_i$ mixed with $\alpha_i$), and verbatim duplication of Figure 3 as Figure 10 in the appendix.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear limitation in existing color-equivariant neural networks (such as LCER), where modeling bounded, interval-valued channels (saturation and luminance) with the translation group leads to clipping and boundary artifacts.

The empirical evaluation is extensive, spanning synthetic datasets (3D Shapes), illumination benchmarks (Small NORB), real-world histopathology (Camelyon17), and multiple image classification benchmarks under distribution shift.

Section 5.5 provides a thoughtful discussion of the inductive bias boundaries and failure modes of color equivariance, explicitly analyzing settings where color is an essential signal (e.g., KUTomaData) or where distribution shifts are absent.
weaknesses: The core mathematical formulation contains fundamental errors. The map $\pi(\theta) = \frac{c}{2}\sin\theta$ is not a topological covering map from $\mathbb{T}^1$ to the closed interval $[-c/2, c/2]$; its derivative vanishes at $\pm \pi/2$, and the fibers over $\pm c/2$ consist of a single point while interior fibers consist of two points (it is a branched cover / folding map, not an evenly covered covering space).

The proposed group action $\varphi_s$ on images (Eq. 8) fails basic group action axioms. First, adding an angle $s_i \in [0, 2\pi)$ directly to a scalar saturation value $x_s \in [0, c]$ mixes incompatible domains. Second, because $\arcsin(\sin(\alpha)) \ne \alpha$ outside $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$, sequential applications do not satisfy composition $\varphi(s_1, \varphi(s_2, x)) = \varphi(s_1 \cdot s_2, x)$. In fact, by topological obstruction, no cyclic group $C_M$ with $M \ge 3$ can act faithfully on a closed interval.

The extension to scale equivariance in Section 6 (Eq. 24) is mathematically unsound. Mapping spatial pixel coordinates $(p_x, p_y)$ through periodic phase shifts inside a sine function has no geometric or operational relationship to scale transformations (dilation $x \mapsto s x$).

The group convolution formulation in Section 4 is incomplete. Eq. (15) and Eq. (16) omit spatial coordinates $\mathbb{Z}^2$ entirely, failing to define how spatial translation and the HSL group action interact (e.g., as a direct product group $\mathbb{Z}^2 \times HSL$).

The computational overhead is prohibitive: Table 12 indicates that full HSL lifting ($T^3\text{CEN-H4S4L4}$) incurs a 32-fold increase in GPU memory (from 1,030 MiB to 32,842 MiB) and a 12-fold drop in throughput (from 19.38 it/s to 1.59 it/s). Furthermore, on in-distribution vanilla datasets (Table 9), $T^3\text{CEN}$ consistently underperforms standard ResNet backbones and established data augmentation baselines.

The manuscript contains substantial presentation and drafting issues: Section 4 is incorrectly titled '4. Background' instead of 'Method'; Appendix D.5 contains an unresolved reference ('shown in Figure '); Table 12 caption contains an incomplete sentence; Section 6 and Figures 7/8 inconsistently refer to '$T^4\text{CEN}$'; Eq. (24) contains an undefined variable $g_i$; and Appendix B spends 15 equations proving the elementary fact that $\mathbb{Z}_N$ is a group while leaving core theoretical claims unproven.

strengths: Addressing the limitation of existing color-equivariant networks—specifically the boundary truncation and zero-padding artifacts encountered when modeling interval-valued quantities like saturation and luminance as translation groups—is a well-motivated research problem.

The paper conducts extensive empirical evaluations spanning synthetic datasets (3D Shapes, Small NORB), real-world transfer benchmarks (CIFAR, Caltech, Stanford Cars, Oxford Pets), and medical imaging (Camelyon17).
weaknesses: Fundamental mathematical flaw in the group action definition: In Equation (8), the action of $s_i \in S_M$ on an HSL image $x = (x_h, x_s, x_l)$ is defined as $\phi_s(s_i, x) = (x_h, \pi((x_s + s_i) \pmod{2\pi}), x_l)$ where $\pi(\theta) = \frac{c}{2} \sin \theta$. First, $x_s \in [0, c]$ is an interval-valued scalar while $s_i \in [0, 2\pi)$ is an angular element, so adding them directly conflates units and domains without defining an explicit inverse map $\pi^{-1}$. Second, and most critically, this does not satisfy the group action axiom $\phi_s(a, \phi_s(b, x)) = \phi_s(a \cdot b, x)$. Applying two successive transformations yields $\pi(\pi(x_s + b) + a)$, which is not equal to $\pi(x_s + a + b)$ because $\pi$ is a sine function rather than the identity. Hence, $\phi_s$ is mathematically not a valid group action on the image space.

Unnatural physical semantics for bounded quantities: Enforcing cyclic boundary conditions via a double-cover $\mathbb{T}^1 \to I$ causes monotonic perceptual attributes like luminance and saturation to oscillate rather than shift monotonically. As admitted in the caption of Figure 1, lifting luminance of a bright background wraps around to produce dark/black representations. Similarly, in Equation (24), applying the double cover $\pi((p_x + \alpha_i) \pmod{2\pi})$ to spatial pixel coordinates does not model geometric scaling (resolution change); instead, it warps and folds pixel coordinates sinusoidally across the canvas. Claiming this constitutes 'scale equivariance' is conceptually incorrect.

Disproportionate and uninformative proofs: The appendix dedicates nearly two full pages (Appendix B.1–B.3, Equations 30–50) to proving that addition modulo $2\pi$ on a uniform grid forms a cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ (an elementary algebraic property). Conversely, the manuscript provides no formal proofs for its central claims: that the proposed lifting layer is equivariant to true saturation/luminance shifts or how the 2-to-1 non-invertibility of the covering map $\pi$ is handled during inference and reconstruction.

Inconsistencies and notation errors in presentation: The text frequently switches notations without explanation (e.g., introducing '$T^4\text{CEN}$' in Section 5.4 and Figure 7 caption while the paper proposes '$T^3\text{CEN}$'). In Equation (24), an undefined variable $g_i$ appears in place of $\alpha_i$ ($"p_x + g_i"$).

Mixed performance on natural images: On clean/unmodified datasets (Table 7), incorporating the proposed equivariant layers often degrades performance compared to standard CNN baselines (e.g., on Oxford Pets, vanilla ResNet achieves 31.52% error while $T^3\text{CEN-L4}$ achieves 41.30%; on Stanford Cars, ResNet-aug achieves 22.38% error while $T^3\text{CEN-S4L4}$ achieves 25.84%). Standard data augmentation (`ResNet-aug`) also outperforms or matches the method on several corrupted benchmarks in Table 5.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant challenge in computer vision: achieving robustness and equivariance to color and photometric shifts (hue, saturation, and luminance) in convolutional networks.

The manuscript provides extensive empirical experiments spanning synthetic benchmarks (3D Shapes, Small NORB), standard vision datasets (CIFAR-10/100, Caltech-101, Oxford Pets, Stanford Cars, STL-10), and real-world histopathology data (Camelyon17).
weaknesses: Fundamental mathematical flaw regarding covering spaces: The map $\pi(\theta) = \frac{c}{2} \sin \theta$ from $\mathbb{T}^1$ to the interval is not a topological covering map. By definition, a covering map must be a local homeomorphism everywhere. At the extrema ($\theta = \pm \pi/2$), the derivative vanishes and the map folds the space, meaning the base space points do not have evenly covered neighborhoods. Calling this a 'topological covering' is mathematically incorrect.

Ill-defined lifting and inverse: In Section 4 (Equation 8), the group action on saturation is written as $\varphi_s(s_i, x) = (x_h, \pi((x_s + s_i) \pmod{2\pi}), x_l)$. However, in standard HSL space, saturation $x_s$ is a real value in an interval $[0, c]$, not an angle in $[0, 2\pi)$. The paper asserts lifting via the 'inverse of the double-cover $\pi$', but because $\pi$ is a 2-to-1 map, its inverse is multivalued. The manuscript never defines how a scalar saturation/luminance value is deterministically lifted to an angle on the circle prior to adding $s_i$. Furthermore, there is an explicit contradiction between Section 4 ($\\pi(\theta) = \frac{c}{2} \sin \theta$) and Appendix A.1 ($\pi(\theta) = c \sin \frac{\theta}{2}$).

Unnatural inductive bias for photometric channels: Enforcing a cyclic group ($S^1$) on non-cyclic, bounded quantities like luminance and saturation introduces severe semantic distortions. As admitted in the caption of Figure 1, as luminance increases past pure white, it wraps around and produces dark gray/black. Imposing cyclic equivalence between bright and dark states contradicts physical optics and breaks the monotonic nature of luminance and saturation.

Flawed formulation of scale equivariance: In Section 5.4 (Equation 24), the authors claim that scale equivariance can be obtained by defining an action on pixel coordinates as $\varphi_\alpha(\alpha_i, x) = (\pi((p_x + g_i) \pmod{2\pi}), \pi((p_y + \alpha_i) \pmod{2\pi}))$. Shifting pixel coordinates inside a periodic sine function does not perform image scaling or downsampling; scaling corresponds to a dilation $(s \cdot p_x, s \cdot p_y)$ or scale-space blurring, not a coordinate phase shift.

Tautological equivariance error evaluation: In Section 5.1, the quantitative equivariance error of $\mathbb{T}^3$CEN ($4.66 \times 10^{-6}$) is computed against the network's own defined cyclic action $\varphi_s$ and $\phi_s$. Since discrete group convolutions over cyclic groups are equivariant to cyclic shifts by construction, showing near-zero error under numerical precision is an identity/tautology, not a meaningful comparison against methods like LCER that model non-periodic translations.

Mathematical and presentation errors: Equation 18 defines partition entropy as $H = \frac{1}{c} \sum v_i \log v_i$, omitting the negative sign required for Shannon entropy (which would yield negative values, yet Figure 5 plots positive entropy). Figure 3 and Figure 9 are identical duplicates. Furthermore, Appendix B expends two pages (Equations 32–46) on trivial proofs that $\mathbb{Z}_N$ under addition modulo $2\pi$ forms a group.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant challenge in computer vision: building neural representations that are robust and equivariant to photometric variations beyond hue (specifically, saturation and luminance), where boundary clipping has historically caused representation degradation.

The empirical evaluation is extensive, spanning synthetic benchmarks (3D Shapes, Small NORB), out-of-distribution shifted image classification datasets (CIFAR-10/100, Caltech-101, Stanford Cars, Oxford Pets, STL-10), and real-world medical histology data (Camelyon17).
The motivation to eliminate zero-padding and boundary truncation artifacts in translation-based color equivariant architectures (such as LCER) is clear and well-articulated.
weaknesses: Fundamental mathematical flaw regarding topological coverings and group actions: The projection $\pi(\theta) = \frac{c}{2} \sin \theta$ is not a topological covering map. By definition, a covering map must be a local homeomorphism (and a local diffeomorphism in the smooth category). At $\theta = \pm \pi/2$, the derivative vanishes ($\pi'(\theta) = 0$) and $\pi$ is not locally injective, meaning it is a branched/folded map rather than a covering space. Furthermore, by topological classification of transformation groups, there exists no non-trivial continuous group action of $S^1$ (or cyclic group $C_M$ for $M \ge 3$) on a compact interval $[0, c]$.

Failure of the group action axioms in Eq. (8): Because $\pi: T^1 \to \tilde{I}$ is two-to-one, it is non-invertible without choosing a branch. In Eq. (8), the group action on images is written as $\phi_s(s_i, x) = (x_h, \pi((x_s + s_i) \pmod{2\pi}), x_l)$. If $x_s \in \tilde{I}$, adding an angle $s_i$ directly to an interval value is dimensionally inconsistent; if $x_s$ is converted to an angle via $\arcsin$, the two-to-one folding implies that $\phi_s(s_j, \phi_s(s_i, x)) \neq \phi_s(s_j \cdot s_i, x)$. Thus, $\phi_s$ does not define a valid group action on the image space.

Unphysical nature of cyclic saturation and luminance shifts: Real-world changes in illumination and saturation are monotonic bounded operations (scaling or dynamic range translation). Imposing a cyclic sine mapping forces saturation to oscillate periodically (e.g., shifting a high-saturation image forward decreases its saturation, folds through zero, and re-emerges). Consequently, the near-zero equivariance error in Figure 3 is tautological—it reflects only the commutativity of the network's internal discrete grid with synthetic test shifts generated using the exact same sinusoidal formula, rather than true physical lighting invariance.

Unsound formulation of scale equivariance: In Section 5.4, Eq. (24) attempts to extend the method to scale by defining the action on spatial pixel coordinates as $\phi_\alpha(\alpha_i, x) = (\pi((p_x + g_i) \pmod{2\pi}), \pi((p_y + \alpha_i) \pmod{2\pi}))$. Passing spatial coordinates through periodic sine functions is a non-linear spatial distortion/warping, not a scale/dilation transformation ($x \mapsto s x$). Additionally, citing Hosu et al. (2025)—an image quality assessment paper—to justify this geometric group formulation is completely inappropriate.

Weak empirical performance against standard data augmentation: On out-of-distribution shifted benchmarks (Table 5), standard data augmentation (ResNet-aug) substantially outperforms $T^3$CEN in several key settings (e.g., Caltech-101 luminance shift: ResNet-aug achieves 30.82% error vs. 46.23% for $T^3$CEN-H4L4; CIFAR-100 saturation shift: ResNet-aug achieves 43.13% error vs. 45.99% for $T^3$CEN-S4L4). Furthermore, on clean/in-distribution datasets (Table 7), $T^3$CEN suffers a significant degradation in accuracy compared to standard ResNets (e.g., error increases from 7.86% to 11.18% on CIFAR-10, and from 32.00% to 40.87% on CIFAR-100).

Disproportionate presentation of elementary proofs: Appendix B dedicates nearly three full pages (Eqs. 30–50) to proving that modular addition on a uniform discretization of $[0, 2\pi)$ forms an abelian group (associativity, identity, inverse), which is standard elementary algebra, while failing to provide a rigorous proof that the proposed operations form a valid group action on the image space.
